On Jan. 18, 1969 we anticipated that 
KLAC "will soon be shopping for new 
turntables - switching from talk to 
music." The station denied the item. 
A few months after they were airing 
Pet Clark, the Fifth Dimension and 
Tony Bennett. And are now denying 
the rumor that they'll switch to a 
somewhat heavier rock format. 
On Feb. 15, 1969 we noted that "Wind- 
mills of Your Mind" was "the song to 
beat" in the Oscar -race. It breezed in 
in April. (This coming year we're bet- 
ting on Rod McKuen's "Jean"). 
On May 31st we suggested that Roy 
Clark's "Yesterday When I was Young 
would be "one of the biggest Dot singles 
in years." It was. '69 was "C" for 
Country year. It was also "C" for 
Cash (Johnny) and Clark (Roy).

come Autumn with the main title theme 
also a chart winner." We batted. 750 
with that one. The U.A. soundtrack got 
no higher than the 20's.

CHICAGO 
Jerry Kaufman of the Sherman House 
is launching an ambitious program of 
"concerts," spotlighting some of the 
biggest night club names in the coun- 
try, to commence in February of next 
year. Series will be presented at the 
Mill Run Playhouse in suburban Niles, 
which has been leased by Kaufman. 
Each concert will run a full week. Lead- 
off bill will feature Eydie Gorme and 
Steve Lawrence, followed by Zsa Zsa 
Gabor, Totie Fields, Sammy Davis Jr. 
and Don Rickles. Negotiations are cur- 
rently underway to book Tony Bennett, 
Wayne Newton, Anthony Newley and 
Buddy Hackett 
. Transamerica's 
Wayne (Big Cat) Juhlin arranged a 
full p.a. schedule last week for song- 
ster Vic Dana who was here to intro 
his new Imperial single "If I Never 
Knew Her Name" 
. 
. 
. Congrats to 
Liberty -UA' promo man Paul Diamond 
and his new bride, the former Merle 
Silverman. Nuptials took place Dec. 14 
at the Sheraton Blackstone Hotel and 
the happy couple are currently enjoy- 
ing a honeymoon in the Bahamas! .. . 
Hammond, Ind. deejay Tony Rugero 
(WJOB) aired an exclusive interview 
with Capitol's Peggy Lee last week! 
. Chi -based 22nd Century Productions 
has chalked up a most successful first 
full concert season, with 86% attendance 
and 84% receipts for the period Oct. 3 
to Dec. 9. Firm's plans for 1970 include 
more concerts, and expansion into 
talent management, retailing and in- 
dustry counseling. Dick Gassen and 
Charlie Witz head up the company 
.

Denmark 
1969 has been a year of two definite 
but not yet overwhelming trends in 
British pop music. One is the progres- 
sive, underground or heavy move- 
ment, and the other is reggae, for- 
merly known as blue beat and ska, 
with Caribbean antecedence. 
The previous year was amorphous in 
terms of trends and the British indus- 
try has welcomed the two newcomers 
with some formidable activity. 
Spe- 
cialist underground labels like Har- 
vest, Vertigo, Threshold and Straight 
have come into being, and there is a 
considerable amount of progressive 
repertoire being recorded or picked up 
on leasing deals for established labels 
virtually everywhere. 
Reggae 
has 
proved profitable for smaller outfits 
like Island and its associates, and 
cornered enough chart action to en- 
courage a giant like EMI to move into 
the same market at the time 
of 
writing. It's most obvious appeal is 
exerted in the West Indian immigrant 
locations, but records by artistes like 
Desmond Dekker, Max Romeo, and 
the Upsetters have sold in quantities 
that prove this essentially dancing 
music with simplified beat and melody 
is reaching a wider and receptive au- 
dience. The Beatles remain the legen- 
dary moneyspinners they have been 
for the past five years, and their 
"Abbey Road" album sales proved 
their contined potency, unaffected by 
John Lennon's eccentricities and lurid 
rumors alleging that Paul McCartney 
has been a zombie for years. The 
Rolling Stones have been equally ef- 
fective during the year if less active. 
Otherwise the group scene spotlight 
has 
swung appreciably 
from 
the 
teenybopper and bubblegum variety 
to the progressive outfits, which cover 
a broad range of activity from the 
highly articulate Moody Blues to the 
solo and group performers in the con- 
temporary folk field. The 25th anni- 
versary of Glenn Miller's demise re- 
vealed a large latent interest in his 
music and 
1970 could see the big 
band return to prominence in some 
form or other, particularly as the 
progressive groups are increasingly 
augmenting their line-up for their 
recording. 
The paucity of exposure for records 
and new artists remains a thorny 
problem for the music business. The 
present administration is firmly set 
against any commercial radio being 
introduced, and appears to be collab- 
orating with the BBC in pre-empting 
the prospects of such stations by 
hurriedly increasing the number of 
local radio stations operated on public 
money 
by 
the 
BBC. 
Roman 
O'Rahilly's projected airborne Caro- 
line TV pirate still has a question 
mark over it in the shape of the 
Marine Broadcasting (Offences) Act. 
Warner -Reprise chief Ian Ralfini ex- 
pressed satisfaction with the year 
from that company's point of view 
and the market generally. "Every- 
body is much more aggressive in their 
promotion and marketing methods 
nowadays" he told Cash Box. "The 
concentration is on LPs, and that con- 
centration will become even stronger 
in 1970". Warner -Reprise realises the 
difficulty of obtaining exposure as 
much as any company and intends 
combating it by bringing over hit 
artists from the States as often as 
possible and promoting concerts and 
fixing TV dates to support their record 
repertoire. 
From the publishing point of view, 
Southern Music's Bob Kingston re- 
flected that sector's concensus 
of 
opinion by rating 1969 as "an average 
sort of year". "It's been neither down 
nor up. The hit parade has had a 
much more varied content, and is 
wide open these days. Anything can 
go it it's good enough, although the 
problems of exposure haven't got any 
better. There's been a further growth 
and 
development 
of 
the 
smaller 
recording companies, and we at South- 
ern are very pleased we launched 
Spark Records when we did." 
Statistics indicate that the single 
disk continues its steady decline, and 
the LP soars upward in sales, par- 
ticularly the budget productions cost- 
ing less than £1. 1970 should see a con- 
tinuation of the slow but sure expan- 
sion in the tape cartridge and musi- 
cassette market. 
Now for a look at the year's events 
month by month as they happened.

GERMANY- 7969 In Review 
The 1969 Year kicked off with good 
news for the record business. Sales 
had increased in 1968 to 500 Million DM 
($140 million) . 
A grand total of 68.9 
million records, an increase of 11.4 
million over the previous year -a per- 
centage increase of LP's of 37.4%. For 
the first time in Germany there were 
more LP's sold than singles: LP's, 33.4 
million; singles 31.9 million (the sale 
of low-priced LP's were much the 
same as those of the normal -priced 
ones). Single record sales rose sig- 
nificantly (+ 17.3%). After stagnation 
for several years, classical music 
sales reached 25% for that year. 
Whereas in other European countries 
it managed 20% and in the USA under 
14% of the total sales. The ratio of in- 
crease 
for 
light -dancing 
numbers 
amounts to 47% and "E" music to 14%. 
Export as well as import showed a 
downward trend. The only upward 
movement was the export of LP's 
(20%). Although it must be taken into 
account that some special import 
firms are not association members 
and therefore not registered in returns. 
The general revival in business in 
West Gemany is naturally bearing 
fruits for the record producers and it 
can be predicted as this that 1969 will 
also be another successful year. 
JANUARY 
A big surprise was that Barry Ryan 
had 
reached the 
top 
spot 
with 
"Eloise," released by Aberbach. Barry 
sang, for the first time in Hamburg, in 
a stage show arranged by the local 
newspaper, "Hamburger Abendblatt". 
His German program, according to 
radio Luxembourg, is heard in West 
Germany each day by 4.4 million 
listeners, including West Berlin. Radio 
Luxembourg reaches daily 4.39 million 
of the over 14 years of age audience. 
(Total population - 46.65 million). 
Altogether 
Radio 
Luxembourg 
is 
heard by 31.1% of the German popula- 
tion each week. 
Hans Rutz, press chief of Deutsche 
Grammophon in Hamburg took over 
direction of the archives production of 
DGG and Dorothee Koehler became 
the new press chief. 
Hans Lieber, president of Teldec, 
celebrated 
his 
70th 
birthday 
in 
January. 
The second German TV station intro- 
duced a German hit parade on the 18th 
of January with Dieter Thomas Heck 
as the master of ceremonies. The tele- 
casts 
have proved 
a 
tremendous 
success. 
Ester and Abi Ofarim received their 
fourth golden disk from Phonogram 
Ton for their "2 in 3". 
Polytel film Ltd., founded in London 
with a large German backing, aims to 
coordinate the European film and tv 
productions and the sales there -from. 
This firm is an associate of the holding 
company Polytel film N.V. located in 
Amsterdam. (An 80% share is held by 
Siemens and Philips and 20% by TV 
Studio Hamburg) . 
Deutsche Grammophon announced 
the founding of a subsidiary, Polydor 
Inc., in New York. This is a base for 
getting a share of the American 
market. 
Jerry 
Schoenbaum 
is 
president. 
Ariola Eurodisc announced that it 
reached second place within German 
record producers in 1968 with 150 Mil- 
lion DM ($40 million) worth of sales.

AUGUST 
The German Radio Exhibition took 
place in 15 halls. The most talked about 
subjects were color tv, cartridges and 
stereo. 
The tv and radio stations transmit 
their most popular music and show 
programs 
directly 
from 
Stuttgart 
with many wellknown German and 
international stars. 
The exhibition 
drew 726,000 visitors. 
Juergen Otterstein follows Larry 
Yaskiel in the management of the 
Antenna PR company, which belongs 
to Polydor and is doing all promo- 
tion and press work for Polydor.

Radio Luxemburg gives away the

artist of the first half year of 1969 in 
the German program. The winners 
are: Peter Alexander, Freddy and 
Adamo. 
Eddie Barclay, owner of the French 
recording 
companies Barclay 
and 
Riviera, opened his German promo- 
tion office for Germany in Hamburg. 
It's managed by Marco Bachmann. 
Barclay records are still distributed 
by the Metronome. 
Electrola took over the distribution 
of Tamla Motown, until now repre- 
sented by BCS in Germany. 
Udo Juergens has started in Ham- 
burg his second and greatest concert 
tour through Germany, which con- 
tinues until middle of 1970 and takes 
him to more than 200 cities.

One of the most important and great 
German music publishing houses had 
two anniversaries: Wiener Boheme, 
50 years, and Ufaton, 40 years. Lead- 
ing manager of both firms, owned by 
the Bertelsmann concern like the 
Ariola-Eurodisc, is Rudolf Foerster. 
Robert Stolz, the last Austrian com- 
poser of the old Vienna operetta school, 
had more than 2 million recordings 
sold of his compositions on record 
from Ariola-Eurodisc.

SEPTEMBER 
The most important event in Sep- 
tember was the IVth International 
Fest of the Popular Song, which took 
place in Rio, from September 25 to 
October 6. The headquarters were at 
Hotel Gloria and the shows were held 
at Maracanazinho, a stadium turned 
into an enormous theater. This fest is 
especially known for its uninhibited 
and involved audience which applauds 
deliriously any music it appreciates 
and boos mercilessly anything that 
doesn't suit its whims. In the national 
phase, the popular vote chose: 
1 - 
Cantiga Por Luciana by Edmundo 
Souto and Paulinho Tapajos; 2 - Razac 
De Paz Para Nao Cantar by Edmundo 
Lage and Alesio de ' Barros; 
3 - 
Juliana 
by 
Antonio 
Adolfo 
and 
Tiberio Gaspar. The jury voted: 
1 - 
Cantiga Por Luciana; 
2 - Juliana; 
3 - Visao Geral by Cesar Costa Filho, 
Ruy Mauriti and Ronaldo Monteiro de 
Souza. As to the International phase, 
the popular vote chose: 
1 - Cantiga 
Por Luciana (Brazil) ; 2 - Love Is All 
(Great Britain) 
by Les Reed and 
Barry Mason; 
3 - Evie (USA) by 
Jimmy Webb. The jury voted: 
1 - 
Cantiga Por Luciana; 2 - Evie; 3 - 
Love Is All. 
OCTOBER 
Right after the IVth International 
Popular Song Fest in Rio, a hard 
cover LP with many songs of the 
National Phase was launched by CBD 
(Philips) - a live recording. Follow- 
ing this, the same diskery, also with 
the Philips label, put into the market 
an LP with 13 of the 40 competing 
songs of the International Phase. 
Fermata diskery has also launched 
an LP with several Fest songs of the 
National and International phases. 
RCA has put forth Martinho da 
Villa's 
"Madrugada, 
Carnaval 
E 
Chuva," which competed in the IV 
International Fest, in a single compact 
which is expected to hit it just as his 
LP did. 
NOVEMBER 
The just released sound track of the 
film "Capitaes da Areia" based on the 
novel by Jorge Amado, features the 
well-known Eliana Pittman singing 
Dorival Caymmi's compositions. 
"Love is All" sung by Malcolm 
Roberts in the Rio Song Fest (3rd 
place) 
is the absolute hit parade 
leader in Sao Paulo, after an ex- 
tremely fast rise. This is a Fermata 
launching, published by RCA. 
RCA 
released an LP with Os In criveis. 
Philips showed its 
new catalogue 
which included the first LP by their 
new artist, Chico Buarque de Holanda 
who will be sending his compositions 
from Italy. 
The heads of Continental Records, 
Alberto Jackson Byington Neto (Pres- 
ident) , 
Miguel Gomez Campodarve 
(Superintendent) and Wilson Rodri- 
ges 
Poso 
(Commercial 
Manager), 
visited the USA and Latin America 
and wound up with the representation, 
for Continental, of two America labels 
and the launching of 15 Brazilian pro- 
ductions in foreign countries. 
We would also like to thank all 
pubberies, diskeries, 
societies 
and 
radio stations which helped us all 
through the year, in a priceless way.

SEPTEMBER 
The most important event in Sep- 
tember was the IVth International 
Fest of the Popular Song, which took 
place in Rio, from September 25 to 
October 6. The headquarters were at 
Hotel Gloria and the shows were held 
at Maracanazinho, a stadium turned 
into an enormous theater. This fest is 
especially known for its uninhibited 
and involved audience which applauds 
deliriously any music it appreciates 
and boos mercilessly anything that 
doesn't suit its whims. In the national 
phase, the popular vote chose: 
1 - 
Cantiga Por Luciana by Edmundo 
Souto and Paulinho Tapajos; 2 - Razac 
De Paz Para Nao Cantar by Edmundo 
Lage and Alesio de 
' Barros; 
3 - 
Juliana 
by 
Antonio 
Adolfo 
and 
Tiberio Gaspar. The jury voted: 
1 - 
Cantiga Por Luciana; 
2 - Juliana; 
3 - Visao Geral by Cesar Costa Filho, 
Ruy Mauriti and Ronaldo Monteiro de 
Souza. As to the International phase, 
the popular vote chose: 
1 - Cantiga 
Por Luciana (Brazil) ; 2 - Love Is All 
(Great Britain) by Les Reed and 
Barry Mason; 3 - Evie (USA) by 
Jimmy Webb. The jury voted: 
1 - 
Cantiga Por Luciana: 2 - Evie; 3 - 
Love Is All.

CBS-ARTONE Benelux Operation has

most successful 
local productions,

I Need You" 
by the

albums by Willy Schobben, Freddy

AUSTRALIA -1969 In Review 
o`F 
sr` 
o 
Q` 
We will preface our review of the 
year's activities with a brief look at 
the local recording industry as applied 
to Australian talent and product. The 
first few months of 1969 were very bad 
for local disks, with few home -titles 
making a breakthrough at all. Then 
in March we saw the release of what 
was to become the number one Aus- 
tralian hit of the year. "The Real 
Thing" for Russell Morris. This was 
followed by a period of relative quiet 
until in June when "Dear Prudence" 
from Doug Parkinson hit for Focus. 
Things went quiet again but came alive 
in August with the release of "Part 
Three Into Paper Walls" c/w "The 
Girl That I Love" from Russell Morris, 
and "One" by Johnny Farnham, both 
of which became giants. There was 
another lull in September, but things 
popped locally in October with the re- 
lease of "Without You" c/w "Hair" 
by Doug Parkinson; "The Star" from 
Ross D. Wylie; "Picking Up Pebbles" 
by Matt Flinders; and the re -issue of 
"She's My Baby" from Johnny O'Keefe 
all of which found a place in the 
big charts across the nation. 
The latter half of 1969 was the most 
successful period ever, in terms of 
chart ratings, for the Australian pro- 
duct and the industry prepares to move 
into 1970 with an air of confidence 
such as we have rarely known before. 
At long last it seems that people in - 
the -trade are now fully aware of the 
vastness of the international market 
and what it has to offer; and this has 
fired a good many record and pub- 
lishing execs with a new brand of 
enthusiasm for local product. In turn 
this enthusiasm and improvement in 
the quality of the product has created 
a .new level of consumer interest which 
is of course the most vital part of the 
business. The one side effect from this 
action and interest at all levels is that 
it tends to 'encourage' the release of 
a few records that perhaps should 
never have been issued in an effort 
to 'grab a bit of the action'. 
The the standard of Australian re- 
cording can be maintained at a level 
comparable with overseas product, 
there is no reason in the wide world 
why some Australian -produced rec- 
ords shouldn't reach hit popularity 
in overseas markets, especially Amer- 
ica and Britain where there is no 
language problem. 
The one dampening feature of the 
Australian market in relation to the 
Australian product is the problem of 
creating national acceptance for our 
own artists and their records. The sit- 
uation is vastly improved over what it 
was say three years ago, but there is 
still a good deal of work to be done 
to establish the best of Australia's 
talent on a truly national scale. 
A 
record should always be judged on its 
merits, and merits alone ... and the 
sooner the whole industry accepts this 
method of judgement the sooner we 
have national names for artists who 
are worthy of such a place in our busi- 
ness.

CANADA -7969 M Review 
Canada's recording industry is show- 
ing every indication of busting out in 
the coming year. The past 12 months 
have been encouraging and in some 
respect disappointing. While the Guess 
Who and Motherlode became interna- 
tional items, the home front failed to 
rally 'round which unfortunately cre- 
ated too much time between hits and 
as the year closes our only notable 
accomplishment is the Guess Who, 
who although still reside in Canada, 
record in the U.S. 
U.S. observers have often pointed 
up the lack of leaders in the Canadian 
recording industry citing this as being 
the most agonizing and formidable 
factor in our non-profit and lack -lustre 
industry. 
However, with the disappointing lull 
there is a happy note. Some record 
companies are reportedly gearing 
themselves for a new push on domes- 
tic product, and are setting aside a 
special Canadian budget and are pre- 
pared to go for broke. It would appear 
that attempts are being made to create 
a recording star system in Canada, 
and fortunately it is on a nationwide 
basis. 
There are those in the industry who 
have been flagwaving for many years 
and not for selfish reasons. They have 
been hammering at the lack of co- 
operation between the record com- 
panies, independent producers and 
radio stations. They have caused a 
wave of controversy which fortunately 
has added importance to the multi- 
million dollar 
Canadian recording 
industry. Being very pro -Canadian, a 
tactic they have borrowed from the 
U.S. is showing indications of paying 
off, and hasn't labelled them anti- 
American, which has always been an 
underlying fear but happily not so. 
One of the stabilizing hands on the 
Canadian recording industry and one 
regarded by many in the industry as 
an exceptionally fine spokesman is 
George I. Harrison, vice president 
and general manager of RCA Limited 
(Record Division). 
Mr. Harrison has been a driving 
force in the development of domestic 
product on all levels of listening. An 
example of his feelings for the country 
and industry generally are contained 
in the following which he penned in 
response to a request from Canda's 
Cash Box rep. 
"The year 1969 was a great year for 
Canadians and I don't mean the world 
famous hockey team. I mean Cana- 
dian recording talent 
. 
. 
. talent that 
is coming into its own at home and 
abroad. Canadians generally seem to 
have lost their self-consciousness and 
are prepared to stand up and be 
counted in the world of international 
recordings. 
"We have realized that the Cana- 
dian record industry does not begin 
and end in the manufacturing plant, 
which turns a lump of raw compound 
into a flat disc with grooves or a tape 
processing unit upon which one sees 
nothing. No 
. 
. 
. the record industry 
begins with imagination and continues 
through the chain of events until it is 
time to imagine another record. 
"The chief ingredient is imagina- 
tion. Imagination by record people 
who find the artist in a hut in Hudson 
Bay or an opera house in Toronto or 
a club in Cape de la Madelaine or a 
concert in Capilano. Imagination by 
the artist who sings or plays the 
music ... imagination by the producer 
and arranger who looks at a raw lead 
sheet and knows how and by whom the 
song can be made to come alive and 
the imagination of the merchandisers 
who make the music easily 
and 
quickly available to the consumer. The 
imagination of the consumers when 
they hear the music to imagine joy, 
comfort and pleasure. The imagina- 
tion that turns the living room into a 
concert hall, a church or a night club. 
Through imagination, an educational 
record can turn a dull classroom into 
a cultural and pleasant seat of learn- 
ing. Through imagination, a record 
can make every customer an impre- 
sario in his own right. 
"Records are a joy -producing busi- 
ness. Life is nothing without music. 
The business is a thrilling business 
and a high risk business. The profits 
are satisfactory when you are right 
and the losses are great when you are 
wrong. It is a complicated business, 
by its very nature, as it grows and 
expands it will become more com- 
plicated . 
. 
. not less complicated. Its 
complex character is derived from a) 
great variances in musical tastes and 
b) the many configurations by which 
the sound of music is carried to the 
home. 
"The success of the business is, 
among other things, due 
to what 
Einstein 
once 
said; 
'Our 
Unholy 
curiosity'. 
"Music is a thrilling business and 
we all know that profits are important, 
yet I like to think that RCA Canada 
legitimately derive pride from the 
knowledge that we contribute some- 
thing to the happiness of humanity 
all over the world. What we produce 
and sell adds to the fullness of life. 
Music is the cordial of a troubled 
breast. Think about it. Today the 
world is more troubled than ever 
and music is needed more 
. 
. 
. 
is 
needed more than ever. 
"Angels make music, sometimes, 
perhaps, raucous devils do but whether 
of angelic or diabolic origin, it is our 
dedicated task to offer recorded music 
and the spoken word to an ever 
growing public. We mingle with this 
task, profit with benefit, business with 
education, the permanent with the 
transitory and fun with inspiration. 
All in all, we believe RCA Records 
have contributed handsomely to the 
success of Canadian talent through the 
years and, in particular, in 1969 and 
we look forward to even bigger and 
greater achievements 
in the 
70's. 
Overture 70 is a great new sound."

JUNE 
The contest "Un Disco Per L'estate" 
has come to an end with the triumph 
of Al Bano (EMI Italiana) performing 
"Pensando A Te" 
(EMI Italiana) , 
which had been at the top of the charts 
for some weeks before the conclusion 
of the contest itself. The second place 
in the final classification was taken 
by "Lisa Dagli Occhi Blu" published 
by El and Chris sung by Mario Tessuto 
(CGD) , who was the discovery of the 
season, repeating the sensation 
of 
Franco IV and Franco I (Phonocolor) 
at the "Disco Per L'estate" of the 
previous year with "Ho Scritto T'Amo 
Sulla Sabbia" published by Leonardi. 
Third, as last year, Orietta Berti 
(Phonogram) with "L'Altalena" pub- 
lished by Sugarmusic. 
In Italy we have something called 
show -contests which are organized by 
different managers, who act as inter- 
mediaries between the music and 
radio and TV industries. The show - 
contests are televised at fixed dates 
which stimulates record producers to 
fix exposures for their new talents. In 
June, soon after the end of "Un Disco 
Per L'estate," there is the beginning 
of "Cantagiro," a show contest. For 
the year which is ending now, "Disco 
Per L'estate" proved to be much 
more successful and paid back much 
more to the record producers than 
"Cantagiro." "Cantagiro," however, 
was responsible for the success of 
"Rose Rosse" published by Sugar - 
music, signed by Massimo Ranieri 
(CGD) and "In Fondo Al Viale" pub- 
lished by Campi, performed by I Gens 
(Det Records) .

successful General Manager of the
